lessons.unit: Unit 1: Resource management (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Food, water and energy: why resources matter and who has them
objectives: Explain why food, water and energy are essential for economic and social wellbeing
Describe global inequalities in the supply and consumption of resources
Define sustainability and conservation

keywords.def: anything from the environment that people use to meet their needs, such as food, water and energy
controlling how a resource is used so it is available now and in the future
using resources in a way that does not stop future generations meeting their needs
protecting and carefully using resources so they are not wasted or damaged
the amount of carbon dioxide produced by a person, product or activity

starter: Say Bismillah. Imagine there is no electricity, no food in the shops and no water from the taps for three days. List three problems this causes.
Name one renewable and one non-renewable energy source.
What does 'finite' mean?

teach.heading: Three vital resources
bullets: Food gives energy for growth, health and work.
Clean water is needed for drinking, hygiene, farming and industry.
Energy powers homes, transport, hospitals and factories.
teach.note: Start from the starter. Pupils should link each resource to both economic wellbeing (jobs, trade, income) and social wellbeing (health, education, quality of life). A child in a home without electricity cannot easily study after dark. Ask: which one could you survive without longest? (Water the shortest, food a few weeks, energy depends on climate.) Note the AQA spec covers all three, then the school studies the water option in depth.

teach.heading: Global inequalities
bullets: Over 2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water.
Hundreds of millions of people go hungry or lack electricity.
High-income countries consume far more energy and food per person.
teach.note: Use approximate statistics from WHO, UN and IEA; state that figures change and the direction matters. Show a world map of GDP per person next to a map of energy consumption per person. Ask pupils to describe the pattern with data and name a continent that is most resource-poor (sub-Saharan Africa). Pupils should avoid blaming people. Inequality is linked to climate, development, conflict and cost.

teach.heading: Why distribution is uneven
bullets: Physical factors: climate, geology, and where resources are found.
Human factors: wealth, technology, trade and political stability.
Some countries have the resource but cannot afford to extract it.
teach.note: Distinguish between physical scarcity (there is not enough) and economic scarcity (there is enough but people cannot access it). For example, Norway has large hydro and oil resources; some African countries have vast untapped solar potential but little infrastructure. This distinction is used throughout the water topic.

teach.heading: Managing sustainably
bullets: Resources are finite or can be damaged, so they need careful management.
Sustainable management means conserving, reusing, recycling and renewing.
Reducing our carbon footprint is part of sustainability.
teach.note: Misconception from earlier teaching: pupils think 'renewable' alone makes something sustainable. A renewable resource can still be used faster than it renews (e.g. groundwater, fish). Sustainable means meeting today's needs without harming the future. Link to Islam: Allah says do not be wasteful (Qur'an 7:31) and humans are khalifah (stewards) on Earth (Qur'an 2:30).

practice: Describe the pattern in the global map showing energy use per person. Use at least two named regions and data.
Explain the difference between a country with physical scarcity and one with economic scarcity of water.
independent: Explain why access to food, water and energy affects a country's wellbeing. (4 marks)
Describe two ways people can manage a resource sustainably. (2 marks)
Stretch: Explain why some countries consume far more resources than others. (4 marks)
exit: Define sustainability in one sentence.
Give one example of economic scarcity.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page summary: three resources, why each matters, and one example of inequality for each.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled map and data table. EAL: key word glossary with pictures. Stretch: compare two countries using GDP per person and energy use per person.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Resource management (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Water surplus and deficit: global patterns and rising demand
objectives: Define water surplus, water deficit and water stress
Describe how water supply varies around the world
Explain why global water consumption is increasing

keywords.def: when water supply is greater than demand
when water supply is less than demand
when demand for water in an area is higher than the amount available
reliable access to enough safe water for health, food and livelihoods
the amount of a resource that is used
removing water from a river, lake or aquifer

starter: Say Bismillah. Define resource management.
Give one reason why people in some countries cannot access clean water.
Name the two types of scarcity: physical and ____.

teach.heading: Surplus and deficit
bullets: Water surplus: more water is available than people need.
Water deficit: demand is greater than supply.
Surpluses: Canada, Brazil, northern Europe. Deficits: North Africa, the Middle East.
teach.note: Show the AQA-style world map showing water surplus and deficit. Pupils must use locations and the map key in a description. Explain that the UK has a surplus overall but a deficit in some parts: the south-east of England is drier and densely populated while the north-west is wetter. Scale matters: a country can have a surplus and still have regions in deficit.

teach.heading: Water stress
bullets: A country is water-stressed if less than 1,700 cubic metres per person a year.
Water scarcity is below 1,000 cubic metres per person a year.
Parts of Egypt, Saudi Arabia and India are under severe stress.
teach.note: Using per-person availability is a common measure. Walk through a calculation: a country with 8,500 million cubic metres of water and 10 million people has 850 cubic metres per person, so it is water scarce. Ask pupils to calculate for two countries. These thresholds are widely used guidelines; present them as such.

teach.heading: Why is demand rising?
bullets: Population growth means more people need water.
Economic development increases industrial and energy use.
Rising living standards mean more showers, appliances and meat in diets.
teach.note: Agriculture is the biggest user globally (around 70 percent of withdrawals), which is often surprising. Industry and domestic use follow. Link meat to water: producing a kilogram of beef takes far more water than a kilogram of vegetables. Ask: which of these three factors is most important in your opinion? and why?

teach.heading: Factors that affect availability
bullets: Climate and seasons control rainfall and evaporation.
Geology decides how much groundwater can be stored.
Pollution and over-abstraction reduce usable water.
teach.note: Prepare pupils for lesson 3. Rainfall is the key physical factor: low rainfall and high evaporation mean less water. Permeable rocks such as chalk store water in aquifers. Human factors: pollution makes water unusable; over-abstraction lowers water tables; lack of money for pipes and treatment limits supply.

practice: Calculate water availability per person: a country with 3,000 million cubic metres of water and 4 million people. Is it water stressed?
Describe the global pattern of water surplus and deficit shown on the map.
independent: Describe the global distribution of water surplus and water deficit. (3 marks)
Explain why water consumption is rising around the world. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain why some areas with high rainfall still experience water stress. (4 marks)
exit: Define water deficit.
Give two reasons why global water consumption is increasing.
lessons.homework: Research the water supply of one country with a deficit and write five facts about why it is short of water.
lessons.send: SEND: annotated map with pre-highlighted regions. EAL: sentence starters for describing patterns. Stretch: examine a per-person data table for 5 countries and rank them by water stress.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Water insecurity and water supply (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: The impacts of water insecurity
objectives: Define water insecurity
Explain how water insecurity affects health, food production, industry and pollution
Describe how water shortages can lead to conflict

keywords.def: when people do not have reliable access to enough safe water
an illness spread through dirty water, such as cholera or typhoid
contamination of the environment by harmful substances
supplying water to crops by artificial means
a dispute between groups or countries over access to water

starter: Say Bismillah. Define water deficit.
State two reasons why water consumption is rising.
Name one factor that affects the availability of water.

teach.heading: Health and water quality
bullets: Unsafe water spreads cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea.
Children are most at risk and may miss school.
Time collecting water, often by women and girls, is lost to work and study.
teach.note: Handle sensitively. Many children in low-income countries die from diseases linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation. Emphasise that the problem is access and infrastructure, not a lack of effort. Link to Islam: Muslims are taught that water is a gift, and the Qur'an says Allah made every living thing from water (21:30).

teach.heading: Food production and industry
bullets: Farming needs a lot of water; shortages cause crop failure and hunger.
Factories need water for cooling, cleaning and manufacture.
Shortages reduce jobs, income and economic growth.
teach.note: Link to lesson 2: agriculture is the largest water user. When irrigation water is cut, yields fall and food prices rise. Industry such as textiles, mining and power generation uses large volumes. Ask: what happens to a country's economy if factories must shut because of drought?

teach.heading: Pollution
bullets: Raw sewage, chemicals and farm fertiliser contaminate rivers and groundwater.
Polluted water cannot be drunk, so effective supply falls.
Pollution harms fish, wildlife and ecosystems.
teach.note: Water quality is part of availability: a river may be full but unusable. Give examples of causes: untreated industrial waste, fertilisers causing algal blooms, sewage in informal settlements. Cleaning water is costly, so poorer areas are hit hardest. Ask pupils to give a three-link chain: pollution, so, so.

teach.heading: Conflict over water
bullets: Rivers cross borders, so upstream use affects downstream countries.
Example: the River Nile flows through eleven countries.
Disputes over dams, such as Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam, raise tensions.
teach.note: Present balanced facts: Ethiopia built the dam to produce electricity and reduce poverty; Egypt depends on the Nile for almost all its fresh water and worries about reduced flow. Talks involve Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan. Pupils should explain why shared rivers cause conflict without taking sides. Water conflict can also occur within countries between farmers and cities.

practice: Make a spider diagram of the impacts of water insecurity under four headings: health, food, industry, pollution.
Explain how a dam on an upstream country's river could cause conflict downstream.
independent: Explain how water insecurity can affect food production. (3 marks)
Explain how water pollution reduces the amount of water available. (3 marks)
Stretch: 'Water shortages are the main cause of conflict between countries.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Name one waterborne disease.
Give one reason why rivers that cross borders can cause conflict.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph of 100 words explaining the link between water insecurity and poverty.
lessons.send: SEND: impact cards to sort into health/food/industry/conflict. EAL: key terms in context with images. Stretch: research one shared river and the countries involved.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Water insecurity and water supply (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Increasing water supply: dams, transfers, desalination and groundwater
objectives: Describe how dams and reservoirs, water transfers, desalination and groundwater abstraction work
Give advantages and disadvantages of each strategy
Choose the most suitable strategy for a given place and justify it

keywords.def: an artificial lake that stores water, usually behind a dam
moving water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit through pipes, canals or tunnels
removing salt from seawater to make fresh water
water stored underground in rocks called aquifers
a narrow, deep hole drilled to reach groundwater

starter: Say Bismillah. Define water insecurity.
Give two impacts of water insecurity.
What is an aquifer?

teach.heading: Dams and reservoirs
bullets: A dam stores river water in a reservoir for use in dry periods.
Dams can also generate hydroelectric power and control floods.
They flood land, move people and reduce water downstream.
teach.note: Remind pupils that dams are big engineering projects with high costs: construction, displacement of communities, loss of habitat and silt building up. Also evaporation from large reservoirs in hot climates wastes water. Ask pupils to give one benefit for a farmer and one cost for a village.

teach.heading: Water transfer
bullets: Pipes, canals or tunnels move water from surplus to deficit areas.
This gives reliable supplies to cities and farmland.
It is expensive, may harm ecosystems and can cause conflict.
teach.note: Link to lesson 2: transfers fix the spatial mismatch between where water is and where people need it. Costs include energy for pumping and the effect on the donor area. Preview the large-scale example in lesson 5: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project.

teach.heading: Desalination
bullets: Seawater is treated to remove salt, using heat or membranes.
Gulf states such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE rely heavily on it.
It is very expensive and uses lots of energy.
teach.note: Desalination suits wealthy, dry, coastal countries with cheap energy. The brine left behind can harm marine life. Ask: why is desalination not widely used in the poorest countries? Mention that solar energy could make it cheaper and more sustainable in the future.

teach.heading: Groundwater abstraction
bullets: Wells and boreholes pump water from aquifers.
It is cheap and quick, and water is often cleaner.
Over-abstraction lowers the water table and may cause land to sink.
teach.note: Groundwater is the main water source for many farms. Aquifers refill very slowly, so pumping faster than rainfall recharges them is not sustainable, which is a good example of how renewable resources can be mismanaged. Bring back the idea in lesson 1 of sustainable use. In coastal areas over-pumping can draw salt water into the aquifer.

practice: Complete a table: strategy, how it works, one advantage, one disadvantage, for four strategies.
Choose the best strategy for a rich desert coastal country and explain your choice.
independent: Explain how a water transfer scheme increases water supply. (3 marks)
Explain one disadvantage of building a large dam. (3 marks)
Stretch: Compare desalination and groundwater abstraction as ways to increase water supply. (6 marks)
exit: Define desalination.
State one problem caused by over-abstraction of groundwater.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain the advantages and disadvantages of increasing water supply by building a dam.'
lessons.send: SEND: strategy diagram cards. EAL: bilingual glossary; speak-then-write practice. Stretch: evaluate which strategy is best for sub-Saharan Africa and explain the cost issues.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Water insecurity and water supply (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Large-scale water transfer: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project
objectives: Locate the Lesotho Highlands Water Project and explain why it was built
Describe how the scheme works
Evaluate its advantages and disadvantages for Lesotho and South Africa

keywords.def: a scheme of dams and tunnels moving water from Lesotho to South Africa
South Africa's most populated and industrial province, containing Johannesburg and Pretoria
electricity generated by the movement of water through turbines
when people are forced to leave their homes, for example because of a dam
a payment made for the use of a resource

starter: Say Bismillah. Name four strategies for increasing water supply.
What is a water transfer?
Give one disadvantage of building a dam.

teach.heading: Why was it needed?
bullets: Gauteng is South Africa's economic heart, with millions of people and many industries.
Gauteng has limited water and high demand.
Lesotho has a surplus of rainwater in its mountains.
teach.note: Locate Lesotho (a small country entirely surrounded by South Africa) and Gauteng on a map. Draw the idea: surplus in the highlands, deficit in the city region. The project was agreed by a treaty between the two governments in 1986, and the first phase delivered water in the late 1990s. Explain how an NEE (South Africa) and an LIC (Lesotho) are both involved.

teach.heading: How does it work?
bullets: Dams such as Katse and Mohale store water in the highlands.
Tunnels carry the water to rivers that flow to Gauteng.
Phase 2 is adding more dams and tunnels.
teach.note: Katse Dam is one of the highest dams in Africa at about 185 metres. Water flows by gravity through tunnels towards the Vaal River system, so little pumping is needed. Draw a simple flow diagram. Check the latest information on Phase 2 (Polihali Dam) in your text before teaching, as construction progress changes.

teach.heading: Advantages
bullets: Reliable water for millions of people and industries in Gauteng.
Lesotho earns money from selling water.
Hydroelectric power gives Lesotho much of its electricity.
teach.note: Ask pupils to separate benefits to South Africa (water security, jobs, industry) from benefits to Lesotho (income, power, new roads). Mention that the project created jobs during construction and improved roads in remote areas. Encourage the use of facts and named places in exam answers.

teach.heading: Disadvantages
bullets: Thousands of people lost homes or farmland and some needed resettling.
Rivers below the dams have less flow, affecting wildlife.
Costs are very high, and compensation was not always adequate.
teach.note: Reservoirs flood valleys and farmland. Reduced downstream flow affects fish and farming communities. The cost is large for a small country, and some people felt benefits did not reach them. Avoid claiming specific numbers unless confirmed in the textbook. Ask: who gained most, and who lost most? Decision-making needs to be fair, a point Islamic ethics also stresses.

teach.heading: Judging success
bullets: Social: improved supply for Gauteng, but displaced communities suffered.
Economic: income and jobs, but very high costs.
Environmental: lost habitats and lower river flows.
teach.note: Teach a balanced SEE framework: social, economic, environmental. A 6-mark answer should have advantages, disadvantages and a final judgement: for example, successful for Gauteng's water security, more mixed for local communities. Model a judgement sentence that begins 'Overall,...'.

practice: Draw a labelled sketch map showing Lesotho, South Africa, Gauteng, and arrows for the water transfer.
Complete a table of advantages and disadvantages by social, economic, environmental.
independent: Explain why the Lesotho Highlands Water Project was built. (4 marks)
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the scheme for the people of Lesotho. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'Large water transfer schemes are the best way to solve water shortages.' Using the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, how far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Which two countries are linked by the Lesotho Highlands Water Project?
Give one disadvantage of the scheme.
lessons.homework: Create a fact file for the project with location, aim, how it works, two advantages and two disadvantages.
lessons.send: SEND: partly completed fact file and map outline. EAL: sentence frames 'The scheme was built because...'. Stretch: compare with another water transfer scheme from your textbook.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Sustainable water management and exam skills (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Sustainable water supplies: conservation, recycling and groundwater management
objectives: Define sustainable water supply and sustainable development
Describe water conservation, grey water recycling and groundwater management
Explain why sustainable approaches are important for the future

keywords.def: providing water in a way that meets present needs without harming future supplies or the environment
using less water and reducing waste
used water from baths, sinks and washing machines that can be reused for flushing or irrigation
controlling how much water is taken from aquifers so they can recharge
economic growth that protects the environment and people for the future

starter: Say Bismillah. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of desalination.
What problem does over-abstraction cause?
In your own words, what does sustainability mean?

teach.heading: Why sustainable?
bullets: Big schemes can be costly and damage ecosystems.
Sustainable approaches meet today's needs without harming the future.
They need to be affordable, fair to people and kind to the environment.
teach.note: Link to the Drive lesson on managing resources sustainably. Use the idea that sustainable solutions must be effective in three areas: social, economic and environmental. Ask: is a project sustainable if it works for 20 years but destroys a river? Connect to the Islamic principle of stewardship (khalifah, Qur'an 2:30) and avoiding waste (Qur'an 7:31).

teach.heading: Water conservation
bullets: Fix leaking pipes and fit water meters.
Use dual-flush toilets, low-flow showers and water-efficient washing machines.
Farmers can use drip irrigation and grow drought-tolerant crops.
teach.note: Leaks in old pipes waste a large share of treated water in some cities. Metering encourages people to use less. Ask pupils which action they could take at home this week. A sustainable action does not need to be expensive: turning off the tap while brushing teeth, or not leaving a tap running while washing up, cuts waste. Keep this light and practical.

teach.heading: Recycling and grey water
bullets: Grey water from sinks and showers can flush toilets or water gardens.
Rainwater harvesting collects roof water in tanks.
Treated wastewater can be used for industry or farming.
teach.note: Explain the difference between grey water (lightly used) and black water (sewage). Rainwater harvesting is cheap and appropriate for homes and villages. Pupils should be able to state a cost and a limit: treatment systems need investment, and people may be reluctant to use recycled water.

teach.heading: Managing groundwater
bullets: Limit abstraction licences so wells do not run dry.
Recharge aquifers by collecting rainfall in ponds and pits.
Protect land above aquifers from pollution.
teach.note: Link to the Thar Desert and Rajasthan from Year 10: johads recharge groundwater. Explain recharge: surface water slowly percolates through the soil to refill the aquifer. Sustainable groundwater use means abstraction does not exceed recharge. Prepare pupils for the next lesson's local scheme.

practice: Sort these actions into conservation, recycling or groundwater management: water meters, grey water for toilets, abstraction licences, drip irrigation, rainwater tanks.
Explain why leakage control is a sustainable way to increase water supply.
independent: Explain what is meant by a sustainable water supply. (2 marks)
Explain how conservation and recycling can help create sustainable water supplies. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate whether sustainable water strategies can solve water shortages in a growing city. (6 marks)
exit: Define grey water.
Give one way a farmer can use water more sustainably.
lessons.homework: Plan a one-week household water-saving challenge with five actions and estimate which saves most water.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards with pictures. EAL: key word bank; speaking frame 'This is sustainable because...'. Stretch: compare cost and effectiveness of three sustainable strategies.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Sustainable water management and exam skills (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Local water scheme in an NEE: the Wakel Basin Project, Rajasthan
objectives: Locate the Wakel basin in Rajasthan, India and describe the water problem
Describe the small-scale techniques used and why they are appropriate technology
Evaluate the scheme and compare it with a large-scale transfer

keywords.def: a river catchment area in Rajasthan, India, where a local water-management project has been carried out
simple, low-cost methods that local people can build and maintain
collecting and storing rainwater for later use
when water seeps down and refills an aquifer
newly emerging economy: a country with rapid economic growth, such as India

starter: Say Bismillah. Define sustainable water supply.
Name one conservation method and one recycling method.
What does appropriate technology mean?

teach.heading: The place and the problem
bullets: Rajasthan is a dry state in north-west India, partly in the Thar region.
Rain falls in a short monsoon; the rest of the year is dry.
Wells were drying up as groundwater was over-used.
teach.note: Link back to the Thar (Year 10): hot, dry, unreliable rain, groundwater falling. Locate Udaipur and the Wakel basin on a map of Rajasthan. Check your class textbook for the exact figures and dates so pupils learn the version used in their exam materials; the points below are the general features of the scheme. Ask pupils why a big dam might not suit remote villages.

teach.heading: What was done?
bullets: Villagers built small earth dams and ponds to catch monsoon rain.
Water soaks into the ground, refilling wells and aquifers.
Local people planned, built and maintained the structures themselves.
teach.note: This is an example of a local, small-scale, bottom-up scheme. The structures are similar to the johads you met in Year 10. Emphasise how they work: slow the runoff, store water, and encourage percolation and recharge. This is an exemplar of appropriate technology: cheap, simple, repairable.

teach.heading: Benefits
bullets: Wells hold water for longer, so drinking water improves.
Farmers can irrigate and grow more crops, raising incomes.
Less time spent walking to fetch water; healthier communities.
teach.note: Ask pupils to group the benefits as social, economic and environmental. Environmental: groundwater rises, vegetation returns, soil erosion reduces. Link to wellbeing: more reliable water improves food security and health. Try to use the language of the mark scheme: 'increases the sustainable supply of water'.

teach.heading: Limitations
bullets: Depends on monsoon rain; a weak monsoon means less water.
Only small areas benefit; it cannot supply a big city.
Needs community cooperation and maintenance over time.
teach.note: A balanced evaluation is crucial. Compare with the Lesotho scheme: Lesotho gives large volumes to millions but costs more, displaces people and relies on outside money. The Wakel scheme is low-cost, local, and sustainable but small scale. Neither is perfect, and the best choice depends on the place and the need.

practice: Complete a comparison table: Lesotho Highlands Water Project vs Wakel Basin Project (scale, cost, who benefits, environmental impact, sustainability).
Explain why the Wakel techniques are 'appropriate technology'.
independent: Describe how a local water scheme increases the sustainable supply of water. (4 marks)
Explain two benefits to local people of a small-scale water scheme. (4 marks)
Stretch: Compare the sustainability of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project and a local scheme such as the Wakel basin. (6 marks)
exit: Name the state in India where the Wakel Basin Project is located.
Give one limitation of a small-scale water scheme.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph arguing whether small local schemes or large dams are better for NEEs.
lessons.send: SEND: scheme diagram with labels to complete. EAL: sentence starters comparing 'whereas' and 'however'. Stretch: evaluate how community involvement affects the long-term success of a scheme.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Sustainable water management and exam skills (AQA 3.2.3 The challenge of resource management)
lessons.title: Exam workshop: managing resources sustainably (6 and 9-mark questions)
objectives: Unpick command words and plan 6 and 9-mark resource management answers
Use named examples and data accurately in extended writing
Self-assess against levels of response and improve an answer

keywords.def: make a judgement about success or importance using evidence on both sides
weigh up factors and say how important each is
give a balanced argument and a clear final judgement
Point, Evidence, Explain: a paragraph structure for extended answers
a real, named example used to support an answer

starter: Say Bismillah. Give two named examples of water-supply schemes studied this term.
State two advantages of a large-scale water transfer.
State one sustainable way to manage groundwater.

teach.heading: Know your command words
bullets: Describe: say what it is like. Explain: give reasons using because/so.
Assess and Evaluate: weigh both sides, then reach a judgement.
To what extent: argue and conclude how far you agree.
teach.note: Ask pupils to highlight the command word and the topic in the question stem. A very common error is describing when asked to explain. Show two versions of the same answer, one that lists facts and one that explains using linking words. Time guide: roughly one mark per minute, so a 6 mark answer takes about 6 to 7 minutes.

teach.heading: Plan an extended answer
bullets: Introduce briefly, then write two to three PEE paragraphs.
Use named places, facts and figures as evidence.
Finish with a clear judgement that answers the question.
teach.note: Model on the board a plan for: 'Assess the success of water management strategies in increasing supply.' Plan: 1 big dam/transfer (Lesotho) with pros and cons; 2 small-scale scheme (Wakel) with pros and cons; 3 judgement depends on scale, cost and sustainability. Make sure pupils see that you can write less but with precise detail and still achieve high marks.

teach.heading: Model answer features
bullets: Level 3 answers are detailed, balanced and well supported by evidence.
Use connectives: because, which means, as a result, however.
Use geographical vocabulary: abstraction, aquifer, appropriate technology.
teach.note: Show a model level 3 paragraph and a level 1 paragraph on the same question and have pupils spot the differences. Lower-level answers tend to be generic, one-sided and without examples. Note in the original Drive lesson that model answers worked best when modelled first and pupils had the key words in front of them at the start. Give them the word bank now.

teach.heading: Self and peer assessment
bullets: Highlight Point, Evidence and Explain in three different colours.
Check: named example, data, balance, judgement.
Write one target for your next answer.
teach.note: This builds exam independence. Pupils swap with a partner and check against the level descriptors. Remind them that checking is about getting better, not being harsh on yourself or a partner. Collect targets to inform the next lessons.

practice: Underline the command word and topic in: 'Evaluate the effectiveness of large-scale water transfer schemes in increasing water supply.' Plan three paragraphs.
Rewrite this weak sentence into a PEE paragraph: 'Dams are good because they give water.'
independent: Using a named large-scale scheme, assess the advantages and disadvantages of increasing water supply by water transfer. (6 marks)
'Small-scale water schemes are more sustainable than large-scale schemes.' To what extent do you agree? (9 marks)
Stretch: self-mark your 9-mark answer and rewrite the conclusion to reach a higher level.
exit: What is the difference between 'describe' and 'explain'?
Name two things a Level 3 answer must include.
lessons.homework: Complete a timed 6-mark question on sustainable water supply, then self-mark it using the levels of response.

lessons.title: Measuring development and the Demographic Transition Model
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we decide whether a country is developed, and how does population change fit?
objectives: Classify countries by level of development and quality of life
Evaluate economic and social measures of development, including GNI, HDI and life expectancy
Link the Demographic Transition Model to development
successCriteria: All: define development and name three measures
Most: explain what GNI and HDI show and their limits
Some: link each DTM stage to development with examples
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: rates, averages and graphs; Science: population and health
lessons.smsc: Social: concern for the wellbeing of all people (rahmah)

keywords.def: the improvement in people's standard of living and quality of life
gross national income divided by population: the average income per person
Human Development Index: combines life expectancy, education and income, scored from 0 to 1
number of live births per 1,000 people per year
number of deaths per 1,000 people per year
deaths of babies under 1 per 1,000 live births

starter: Bismillah. Define resource and give an example.
Which is more densely populated: a city or a rural area? Why?
Name one country you think is a high-income country and one a low-income country.

teach.heading: Classifying countries

head: Group
Meaning
Example
rows: High-income country: high GNI per person, advanced services
Newly emerging economy: rapid growth, industrialising
Low-income country: low GNI, mainly primary industry

teach.note: Explain that the old terms 'developed/developing' are replaced by HIC, LIC and NEE. World Bank income groups use GNI per capita; thresholds change each year (approx. FY2025: low income about $1,145 or less; high income above about $14,005; teacher to check current). NEE: fast-growing industrial economy, for example China, India, Nigeria, Brazil. Misconception: development is only money.

teach.heading: Measures of development
teach.note: Ask pupils which measure tells most about quality of life and which is easiest to compare. GNI per capita is an average that hides inequality. HDI mixes income, education and health, ranges 0 to 1. Teacher: update HDI figures from the UNDP annual report. As a guide, Switzerland and Norway are near 0.97 and Somalia and South Sudan below 0.4 (approx.).

teach.heading: The Demographic Transition Model

timeline.label: Stage 1
timeline.text: High birth and death rates; population low and steady

timeline.label: Stage 2
timeline.text: Death rate falls, birth rate stays high; rapid growth

timeline.label: Stage 3
timeline.text: Birth rate falls; growth slows

timeline.label: Stage 4
timeline.text: Low birth and death rates; population high and stable

timeline.label: Stage 5
timeline.text: Birth rate below death rate; population may fall

teach.note: Describe each stage and give examples (stage 2 and 3: many NEEs, such as Nigeria which is early stage 2 to 3 in birth rate, flagged as approx.; stage 4: UK; stage 5: Japan, Germany). Explain: death rates fall first (medicine, sanitation, food), birth rates fall later (contraception, women's education, urbanisation). Misconception: the DTM predicts exactly the same path for every country.

teach.heading: Check understanding

check.q: In which DTM stage does the death rate fall while the birth rate remains high?
check.why: Stage 2 is the rapid growth stage: death rates fall due to better health and food, but birth rates stay high. Stage 3 has falling births.

teach.note: Answer C. A is stage 1; B is stage 2; D is stage 4 with some fall. Watch for pupils selecting B because a wide pyramid base suggests growth; they must note falling birth rate.

teach.heading: Linking DTM to development

model.problem: Explain why birth rates fall as a country develops. (4 marks)
steps: Better healthcare means fewer children die, so parents need fewer births.
More girls attend school and women enter work, delaying marriage and childbearing.
Contraception becomes available.
Urban living makes children costly rather than farm helpers.
model.answer: Development improves health, education and women's choices, so birth rates fall.

teach.note: Show the link: as a country develops, healthcare, education and women's rights improve, so birth rates fall. Ask: why do some LICs stay in stage 2 for longer? (Poverty, cultural views of family size, lack of education.) Model the reasoning chain.

practice: State two measures of development and give one limitation of each. (4 marks)
Describe the difference between an LIC and an NEE. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain why GNI per capita alone is not a good measure of development. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain why death rates fall before birth rates in the DTM. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate which measure gives the best picture of a country's quality of life. (6 marks)
exit: What does HDI combine?
Which DTM stage has a falling death rate and high birth rate?
lessons.homework: Choose two countries, find GNI per capita, life expectancy and HDI, and write which is more developed and why.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards for measures and meaning. EAL: bilingual glossary. Stretch: construct your own development index.

lessons.title: Why is development uneven? Causes and consequences
lessons.bigQuestion: What holds some countries back, and what are the effects?
objectives: Explain physical, economic and historical causes of uneven development
Explain the social, economic and political consequences
Describe the link between development and migration
successCriteria: All: name two causes and one consequence
Most: explain physical, economic and historical causes
Some: evaluate which cause is most important
lessons.crossCurricular: History: colonialism and trade; Science: tropical disease
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice and fair trade (adl)

keywords.def: a raw material such as crops or minerals
control of one country by another, often taking its resources
money owed to other countries or banks
a rule, tax or quota limiting imports
a country with no coastline

starter: Bismillah. Name three measures of development.
What is DTM stage 2?
Define primary industry.

teach.heading: Physical causes
bullets: Landlocked countries have higher trade costs.
Tropical diseases such as malaria reduce productivity.
Droughts, floods and earthquakes damage economies.
Few natural resources or poor soils.
teach.note: Be careful of determinism: geography matters but is not destiny. Singapore has few natural resources but is rich. Ask pupils to find counter-examples of landlocked rich countries (Switzerland).

teach.heading: Economic causes
bullets: Reliance on exporting low-value primary products.
Prices for raw materials fluctuate.
Debt payments take money from health and schools.
Trade barriers and subsidies in HICs limit LIC exports.
cycle: Debt payments reduce spending on health and schools
Low productivity: little to invest in industry
teach.note: Use the multiplier idea: processed goods earn more than raw ones (e.g. coffee beans versus roasted coffee). Many LICs spend more on debt payments than on health (state as general; teacher to quote Jubilee Debt Campaign data). Ask: why are manufacturing and services more reliable than primary exports?

teach.heading: Historical causes

timeline.label: 1500s-1800s
timeline.text: Slave trade and colonisation shape Africa, Asia and the Americas

timeline.label: 1800s
timeline.text: Colonies supply raw materials for industries in Europe

timeline.label: 1950s-60s
timeline.text: Many countries gain independence, often with weak infrastructure

timeline.label: 1980s
timeline.text: Debt crises across Africa and Latin America

timeline.label: Today
timeline.text: Uneven trade and debt still shape development

teach.note: Teach with care and evidence. Colonialism: many countries were governed to supply raw materials, and borders were drawn by colonial powers. The transatlantic slave trade removed millions of people from Africa. Conflict after independence often slowed growth. Pupils should state factors without blaming individuals. Link to Islamic ethics of justice (adl) and fair dealing.

teach.heading: Consequences of uneven development

head: Type
Consequence
Example link
rows: Low incomes, low tax, few services

teach.note: Use the table, and ask pupils to explain the links (e.g. poor health reduces workforce). Migration: skilled workers (nurses, doctors) leave an LIC (brain drain), while remittances send money back. Ask: is migration a cause or consequence? (Both.) Good examples: remittances are a major part of income for several countries (teacher to quote World Bank data).

teach.heading: Check and apply

check.q: Which is an economic cause of uneven development?
options: Dependence on exporting raw materials with unstable prices
check.why: Dependence on primary exports is an economic cause. An earthquake and being landlocked are physical; colonial boundaries are historical.

teach.note: Answer B. Use C to discuss: aid may help but is not a cause. Ask pupils for a historical factor.

teach.heading: Model: explain a cycle

model.problem: Explain how debt can keep a country poor. (4 marks)
steps: Low-income countries borrow money to build infrastructure.
Debt repayments take a large share of government income.
Less money is left for schools, health and roads.
With a weaker workforce and poor infrastructure, growth is slow, so more borrowing is needed.
model.answer: Debt repayments reduce spending on development, creating a cycle of poverty.

teach.note: Model writing a developed answer in three sentences, then ask pupils to improve it with a place name.

practice: Give two physical and two economic causes of uneven development. (4 marks)
Explain one consequence of uneven development for health. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how historical factors have affected development in one region. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how migration can be both good and bad for an LIC. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess which factor (physical, economic or historical) is most important in explaining uneven development. (6 marks)
exit: Name one physical cause.
What is the brain drain?
lessons.homework: Research the main exports of one LIC and write why this might limit development.
lessons.send: SEND: cause-effect sort. EAL: key word cards. Stretch: research the Jubilee 2000 campaign.

lessons.title: Reducing the development gap: strategies and tourism in Jamaica
lessons.bigQuestion: Which strategies work best to reduce the gap, and can tourism help?
objectives: Describe and evaluate strategies: investment, aid, Fairtrade, debt relief, microfinance, intermediate technology
Explain how tourism growth in an LIC/NEE can reduce the development gap
Evaluate benefits and costs using Jamaica
successCriteria: All: describe three strategies
Most: explain advantages and disadvantages
Some: evaluate tourism's contribution to reducing the gap
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: trade and enterprise; Economics: multipliers
lessons.smsc: Moral: charity and fair trade; sadaqah as benefit to the poor

keywords.def: help given to a country by governments or organisations, such as money, goods or expertise
a scheme that guarantees farmers a minimum price and a premium for community projects
cancelling or reducing a country's debt
very small loans to poor people to start small businesses
simple, affordable technology that suits local needs
when money spent in one place creates more jobs and income elsewhere

starter: Bismillah. Give two causes of uneven development.
Define debt.
What is tourism?

teach.heading: Strategies to close the gap

head: Strategy
How it helps
Limit
rows: Dependency; may be tied to donor goods

teach.note: Work through the table. Ask pupils to rank by effectiveness and justify. Real examples: Grameen Bank (Bangladesh) microfinance, whose founder Muhammad Yunus won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006; Jubilee 2000 campaign and later G8 debt cancellation (2005); Practical Action intermediate technology (for example pedal-powered or hand-operated pumps). Misconception: aid always helps. Tied aid and corruption can limit benefits.

teach.heading: Check: match the strategy

check.q: A woman in Bangladesh borrows a small sum to buy a sewing machine. Which strategy is this?
check.why: Microfinance gives very small loans to people who cannot access banks. The other strategies work at national or company level.

teach.note: Answer C. A is aid; B is investment; D debt relief. Ask pupils to justify why microfinance fits the description.

teach.heading: Tourism in Jamaica
bullets: Jamaica: Caribbean island, an upper-middle-income NEE.
Tourism is one of its largest earners and employers.
About 2.7 million stopover visitors in 2019 (approx.).

timeline.label: 1960s
timeline.text: Tourism grows after independence in 1962

timeline.label: 1980s
timeline.text: All-inclusive resorts expand
About 2.7 million stopover visitors (approx.)
COVID-19 collapses tourist numbers

timeline.label: After 2021
timeline.text: Recovery, but storms remain a risk

teach.note: State that figures are approximate and the teacher should update from the Jamaica Tourist Board. Draw out multiplier: hotels need food, laundry, taxis, craft sellers. Ask: what attracts tourists? (Beaches, nature, culture.) Jamaica lies in the hurricane belt (Hurricane Beryl passed close in July 2024; verify), so storms are a recurring risk to tourism.

teach.heading: Evaluating tourism
teach.note: Use the compare to build a 6-mark judgement. Draw out leakage: profits of foreign-owned resorts leave Jamaica. Environmental costs: coral damage, waste. Ask pupils: how could ecotourism reduce costs? Model the judgement.

teach.heading: Model: how tourism reduces the gap

model.problem: Explain how tourism growth can reduce the development gap in an LIC or NEE. (4 marks)
steps: Tourists spend money on hotels, food and excursions: income for the country.
This creates jobs, so more people have wages and pay tax.
Governments use taxes to improve roads, schools and clinics.
The multiplier effect: workers spend wages locally, creating more jobs.
model.answer: Tourism brings money, jobs and tax, which pay for services that improve development.

teach.note: Write along, emphasising chain reasoning.

practice: Describe two strategies used to reduce the development gap. (2 marks)
Give one disadvantage of aid. (1 mark)
independent: Core: Explain how Fairtrade helps farmers. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain one cost of tourism for an NEE. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate how far tourism has reduced the development gap in Jamaica. (6 marks)
exit: Define microfinance.
Name one benefit and one cost of tourism.
lessons.homework: Write a short advert for ecotourism in an LIC or NEE explaining how it helps local people.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards and a pre-structured table. EAL: key words with images. Stretch: compare Jamaica with a country where tourism is a smaller part of the economy.

lessons.title: Nigeria: an NEE case study of context, economy and quality of life
lessons.bigQuestion: How is Nigeria changing, and who benefits?
objectives: Locate Nigeria and explain its importance
Describe its economy, TNCs, aid and environmental impacts
Evaluate changes in quality of life
successCriteria: All: locate Nigeria and give two facts
Most: explain how industry, TNCs and aid affect Nigeria
Some: evaluate economic growth against environmental and social costs
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: resources and trade; Citizenship: global links
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of the environment and fairness in sharing wealth

keywords.def: transnational corporation: a company operating in several countries
oil released into the environment, damaging land and water
money sent home by migrants working abroad
gross domestic product: total value of goods and services produced

starter: Bismillah. Define NEE.
Name one measure of development.
Name two TNCs you know.

teach.heading: Context: where and what
bullets: West Africa, on the Gulf of Guinea; borders Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
Population over 200 million (approx.): Africa's most populous country.
Capital Abuja; largest city Lagos.

head: Fact
Detail (approx.)
rows: Crude oil (historically about 90% of export earnings)
English official; Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo widely spoken

teach.note: Use an atlas. State that Nigeria has about 220 million people (approx. 2023, check UN). Ask: why is Nigeria important in Africa? (Population, economy, oil, culture.) Mention colonial history: British control until independence in 1960. Ask pupils to locate neighbouring countries and the Niger Delta.

teach.heading: Economy and TNCs

right.title: TNC costs
points: Oil spills in the Niger Delta

teach.note: Explain: oil drives export earnings and government revenue, but employs few people. Manufacturing and services (telecoms, banking, film, tech) are growing. TNCs: Shell has operated in the Niger Delta for decades, and others such as Unilever, Nestle, Guinness and MTN operate there (teacher to verify current ownership; Shell has been selling onshore assets). Benefits: jobs, tax, technology. Costs: profits leave the country, environmental damage, weak local ownership.

teach.heading: Aid and environment

timeline.text: Oil discovered in the Niger Delta
Independence from Britain
Capital moved from Lagos to Abuja
UNEP Ogoniland report on oil pollution
Nigeria declared free of wild polio (check)

teach.note: Aid: Nigeria receives aid from UK and other donors, and NGO health and education projects, e.g. polio eradication campaigns (Nigeria was declared free of wild polio in 2020, approx. verify). Environment: the UNEP 2011 assessment of Ogoniland found widespread oil pollution and said a clean-up could take 25 to 30 years. Pupils should explain the link between oil pollution, fishing and farming incomes.

teach.heading: Quality of life

check.q: Which statement best describes Nigeria as an NEE?
options: It is growing economically but with inequality and environmental costs
It has the highest HDI in Africa
check.why: Nigeria is growing but with large inequalities and pollution. The other statements are false.

teach.note: Show a mixed picture: HDI roughly 0.55 (approx., UNDP; low human development band), life expectancy around 53 to 54 years (approx.), and large differences between north and south and rich and poor. Pupils should avoid single stories: Nigeria has world-famous film, publishing and technology firms. Use the check to test understanding of NEEs.

teach.heading: Model: a 6-mark evaluation

model.problem: Assess the impact of TNCs on Nigeria. (6 marks)
steps: Positive: TNCs such as oil and telecom companies provide jobs, taxes and technology.
Positive: foreign investment can fund roads and power projects.
Negative: oil spills in the Niger Delta damaged fishing and farming; the UNEP Ogoniland report said clean-up could take 25 to 30 years.
Negative: profits leave Nigeria and the economy is exposed to oil price falls.
Judgement: TNCs contribute to growth, but benefits are uneven and environmental costs fall on local people.
model.answer: A balanced judgement referring to both benefits and costs.

teach.note: Show the three-part structure: advantages, disadvantages, judgement.

practice: Describe the location of Nigeria. (2 marks)
State two ways TNCs can benefit Nigeria. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how oil extraction has caused environmental problems in Nigeria. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how aid can improve quality of life in Nigeria. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the extent to which quality of life has improved in Nigeria. (6 marks)
exit: Name one TNC operating in Nigeria.
What is the main export of Nigeria?
lessons.homework: Prepare a fact file on Nigeria with five facts and a source for each.
lessons.send: SEND: fact file template. EAL: bilingual keywords. Stretch: compare Nigeria with another NEE (India).

lessons.title: UK economic change: de-industrialisation, globalisation and a post-industrial economy
lessons.bigQuestion: How and why has the UK's economy changed since 1950?
objectives: Explain de-industrialisation, globalisation and the rise of the post-industrial economy
Describe the role of science parks, business parks and policy
Explain how modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable
successCriteria: All: define de-industrialisation and name two causes
Most: explain the growth of the post-industrial economy
Some: evaluate the impact of change and the sustainability of modern industry
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Industrial Revolution and Thatcher-era change; Business Studies: industry sectors
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship in industry (khalifah)

keywords.def: the decline of traditional manufacturing industry
growing connections between countries through trade, investment and technology
an economy based mainly on services and technology rather than manufacturing
knowledge-based industries such as research and IT
a group of high-tech firms working together near a university

starter: Bismillah. Name the four sectors of industry.
What does TNC stand for?
Give one example of a service job.

teach.heading: De-industrialisation: causes
bullets: Cheaper manufacturing overseas, especially in NEEs.
Closure of coal mines and heavy industry.
Lack of investment in older factories.
Automation reduced jobs.

timeline.label: 1950s
timeline.text: Manufacturing is a third of jobs (approx.)

timeline.label: 1970s-80s
timeline.text: Closures in steel, shipbuilding and coal
Miners' strike and pit closures

timeline.label: 1990s
timeline.text: Service sector and call centres grow

timeline.label: Today
timeline.text: Services are around 80% of jobs (approx.)

teach.note: Place on timeline. Teacher: manufacturing was about a third of UK employment in the 1950s and is now under 10% (approx., ONS). Ask: which regions lost most? (North of England, South Wales, central Scotland.) Misconception: manufacturing has disappeared; the UK still manufactures high-value goods (aerospace, pharmaceuticals).

teach.heading: Globalisation and the post-industrial economy

head: Change
Example
Effect on UK
rows: Finance in the City, call centres

teach.note: Link globalisation to TNCs and improved transport and communications: 'shrinking world'. UK services include finance, law, creative industries and education. Use the table. Ask pupils: why is London's financial role helped by time zones? (Between Asia and the Americas.)

teach.heading: Science parks, business parks and policy
bullets: Science parks: high-tech research linked to universities, such as Cambridge.
Business parks: offices on edge-of-city sites, good for road links.
Policy: enterprise zones, regional investment and devolved city regions.

check.q: Which best describes a post-industrial economy?
options: Based mainly on services and technology rather than manufacturing
check.why: A post-industrial economy relies mainly on services and high-tech industry. It still has some manufacturing.

teach.note: Mention regeneration in Salford (MediaCityUK, BBC relocated from 2011) and the Northern Powerhouse idea (2014). Be neutral: policy effects are debated. Ask: why locate near a motorway and a university? Check understanding.

teach.heading: Making modern industry more sustainable
teach.note: Use Nissan Sunderland as an example (teacher to verify current details): electric vehicle production including battery manufacturing, on-site solar panels and wind turbines, recycling of materials. Siemens Gamesa's blade factory in Hull (opened 2016) is another example of green manufacturing. Ask pupils to apply: reduce, reuse, recycle, renew.

teach.heading: Model: explain the change

model.problem: Explain how globalisation led to de-industrialisation in the UK. (4 marks)
steps: Transport and communication improved, so firms could produce anywhere.
TNCs moved production to NEEs where wages are lower.
UK factories closed because they could not compete on cost.
Jobs were lost in traditional manufacturing areas such as the North.
model.answer: Globalisation lets TNCs move production overseas, causing factory closures and job loss in the UK.

teach.note: Pupils copy the chain and then substitute their own example.

practice: Describe two features of the post-industrial economy. (2 marks)
Give two causes of de-industrialisation in the UK. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how a science park supports economic growth. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how modern industry can be more sustainable. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impact of de-industrialisation on one region of the UK. (6 marks)
exit: Define post-industrial economy.
Name one TNC that has invested in the UK.

lessons.title: Rural change, the north-south divide and the UK's links with the world

objectives: Describe rural change and explain the causes in an accessible and a remote area
Explain the north-south divide and strategies to reduce it
Describe the UK's trade, cultural and political links
successCriteria: All: describe two rural changes
Most: explain the north-south divide with evidence
Some: evaluate the importance of the UK's links with the wider world
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Commonwealth and the EU; Citizenship: UK in the world
lessons.smsc: Social: good neighbourliness in communities (jiwar)

keywords.def: movement of people from cities to the countryside
the economic and social differences between the north and south of the UK
a group of 56 countries, mostly former British colonies
passing power from national to regional governments

starter: Bismillah. Define counterurbanisation.
Give one UK region hit by de-industrialisation.
Name one type of service industry.

left.title: Accessible rural area
points: House prices rise: young locals priced out
Science and business parks, for example near Cambridge

right.title: Remote rural area
points: Loss of shops, schools and buses
Farming and tourism are main jobs

teach.note: Contrast an accessible rural area (for example South Cambridgeshire, with commuting to Cambridge) and a remote rural area (for example the Scottish Highlands). Teacher to choose and verify a named example. Accessible: population grows, house prices rise, villages become dormitory settlements. Remote: ageing population, loss of services (bus, school, shop) and slower growth. Ask: is counterurbanisation good for everyone?

teach.heading: The north-south divide
teach.note: Describe the pattern: higher incomes, house prices and productivity in London and the South East; lower in parts of the North and Wales, with exceptions. Causes: de-industrialisation, concentration of finance and government in the South, transport and investment differences. Use data from the ONS (teacher to insert the latest GVA per head and life expectancy figures). Warn against stereotypes.

teach.heading: Reducing the divide

check.q: Which strategy aims to reduce the north-south divide?
options: Locating media and public jobs in northern cities
Banning new housing in the north
check.why: Relocating media and public bodies, such as the BBC to Salford, brings jobs to the North. The other options would widen the gap.

teach.note: Strategies: devolution (combined authorities), investment in transport and broadband, enterprise zones, relocating public bodies and media (BBC to Salford in 2011). Criticism: results are slow and uneven. Ask: how could technology reduce the gap? (Remote work.) Check.

teach.heading: The UK's links with the wider world

head: Link
Examples

Commonwealth migration, English language, global media and sport
UN Security Council, NATO, G7, Commonwealth
TNC investment in and from the UK

teach.note: Cover trade, cultural and political links in a table. State trade shares as approx.: the EU remained the UK's largest trading partner after Brexit (31 January 2020 exit; transition ended 31 December 2020), with around 40+% of exports (approx., ONS). The UK is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, a member of NATO, the G7 and the Commonwealth. Culture: English language, music, Premier League, universities.

teach.heading: Model: write a judgement

model.problem: Assess the importance of the UK's links with other countries. (6 marks)
steps: Trade: exports of cars and services bring income and jobs.
Investment: foreign firms like Nissan employ UK workers.
Political: UN, NATO and the Commonwealth give influence and security.
Cultural: migration and languages enrich the economy and society.
Limit: dependence on others can cause risks, for example supply chain disruption.
Judgement: links are vital to the economy, but resilience needs diverse partners.
model.answer: Links are important for trade and influence, though dependence brings risk.

teach.note: Model an answer showing how two sides are weighed.

practice: Describe two changes in a rural area you have studied. (2 marks)
State two UK political links with other countries. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain why house prices are higher in the south than in the north. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain why some remote rural areas have an ageing population. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of one strategy to reduce the north-south divide. (6 marks)
exit: Define north-south divide.
Name one Commonwealth link.

Describe water supply matching and the changing energy mix

large-scale, commercial, industrialised farming run like a business
the proportion of energy supplied from each source
moving water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit
farming without artificial chemical fertilisers and pesticides

Year-round demand for seasonal foods such as strawberries and green beans increases imports.
Organic and local food sales have grown, but remain a small share.

head: Problem
Explanation
Management

Pollution from farms and storm overflows

teach.note: UK average use is around 140 to 145 litres per person per day (approx.). Demand rises with population and appliances. Supply: rainfall is highest in the north and west (Wales, Lake District, Scotland) while demand is highest in the south east, so water must be transferred: Elan Valley reservoirs (opened 1904) supply Birmingham by aqueduct; Kielder Water in Northumberland supports north-east England and can transfer to other rivers (verify). Quality issues: sewage overflows and farm run-off.

teach.heading: Energy: the changing mix

timeline.text: Coal supplies about two-thirds of electricity (approx.)
North Sea oil production peaks
Climate Change Act passed
Coal still about 40% of electricity (approx.)
Last UK coal power station closes; wind and other renewables around 40% (approx.)

teach.note: Use the timeline. Coal supplied about two-thirds of UK electricity in 1990 (approx.) and the last coal power station (Ratcliffe-on-Soar) closed on 30 September 2024. North Sea oil production peaked in 1999. Renewables, especially wind, supply around two-fifths of electricity (approx. 2023). The Climate Change Act (2008) set legally binding targets, later strengthened to net zero by 2050. Teacher to verify current percentages.

teach.heading: Check understanding

check.q: Which statement best describes the change in the UK energy mix since 1990?
options: Coal has declined and renewables such as wind have grown
check.why: Coal use has fallen to zero in power stations while wind and other renewables have grown. Gas remains important.

teach.note: Answer B. Check by asking why A is wrong: coal has declined. D is false; the UK still imports gas.

teach.heading: Model: explain a change

model.problem: Explain why the UK imports a large amount of food. (4 marks)
steps: Demand for foods that cannot grow in the UK climate, such as bananas, is high.
Consumers want seasonal foods such as strawberries all year round.
Supermarkets import from cheaper, warmer countries.
The UK population is too large to be fed only by home production, so imports fill the gap.
model.answer: Climate, year-round demand, supermarket buying and population size lead to imports.

teach.note: Show the cause-and-effect chain. Ask pupils to find a similar chain for water demand.

practice: State what is meant by food miles. (1 mark)
Describe two changes in the UK energy mix since 1990. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain why water must be transferred from the north and west to the south east. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of buying local food. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess how sustainable the UK's energy mix is today. (6 marks)
exit: Define agribusiness.
Which part of the UK has the greatest water surplus?
lessons.homework: Look at your family's weekly food shopping: list five items, where they came from and the likely food miles.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards for local and imported items. EAL: key vocabulary. Stretch: calculate the carbon footprint of a local and an imported item using a footprint calculator.

an extreme food shortage causing widespread starvation and death
a unit of energy in food; average adult needs about 2,000 to 2,500 per day

Give two ways the UK imports food.
What is a calorie?

Many LICs, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, have deficits.
About 733 million people faced hunger in 2023 (FAO, approx.).

Calorie supply (approx.)
Pattern

teach.note: Show a world map of daily calories per person. Typical figures: the USA over 3,500 kcal per person per day (approx.) while some low-income countries are around 2,000 or below. Teacher to verify with FAO. Emphasise average supply masks inequality within countries. Hunger affects about 1 in 5 people in Africa (approx., FAO 2024).

bullets: World population passed 8 billion in 2022.
Rising incomes lead to more meat and dairy.
Meat uses much more land and water than crops.
Urban lifestyles raise demand for processed food.
cycle: Diets shift to meat and dairy
More land, water and feed needed
teach.note: Ask pupils to connect: more people, more money, different diet. Teacher to introduce the idea of food chains: producing 1 kg of beef takes many kilograms of feed. Check the demand side before moving to supply.

head: Factor
Effect on supply
rows: Farmers displaced and food routes blocked
Little access to fertiliser and irrigation

teach.note: Use the table. Link physical (climate change, drought, pests and disease), human (conflict, poverty, poor storage and transport) and economic factors (prices, trade). teach.heading: Impacts of food insecurity

quote.text: Eat and drink, but do not be wasteful.
quote.source: Qur'an 7:31 (meaning paraphrased; use the school's approved translation)

teach.note: Use the Ethiopia famine of 1984-85 as an example: drought and civil war led to an estimated one million deaths (approx.). In 2007-08 and 2010-11 world food prices spiked and were linked to protests and unrest in several countries (the 2011 Arab uprisings had multiple causes). Soil erosion follows overgrazing and deforestation. A teacher may use the quote to link ethics.

teach.heading: Check and model

check.q: Which is an impact of rising food prices in LICs?
options: Poorer households eat less and unrest may increase
check.why: Higher prices hit poor families who spend most income on food and can trigger unrest. Farmers do not always benefit, and imports become dearer.

teach.note: Answer C. Then use the model to practise the structure.

teach.heading: Model: assess the impacts

model.problem: Assess the impacts of food insecurity. (6 marks)
steps: People: undernutrition weakens children and adults, and famine kills.
Economy: weak workers and high prices reduce output and income.
Environment: desperate farmers over-graze and cause soil erosion.
Society: price spikes can lead to unrest, as in 2007-08.
Judgement: the most serious impact is on health because it limits future development.
model.answer: Food insecurity affects people, economy and environment; the health impact is most serious.

teach.note: Teach the pattern: impacts on people, environment, economy.

practice: Describe the global pattern of calorie supply shown in the table. (2 marks)
Explain two reasons for rising food consumption. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain two factors that reduce food supply in an LIC. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how food insecurity can cause soil erosion. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impacts of food insecurity. (6 marks)
exit: Define food security.
Give two causes of famine.
lessons.homework: Find one current news story on food insecurity and summarise causes and effects in 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND: cause-effect matching. EAL: key vocabulary with images. Stretch: link food prices to energy prices.

Explain sustainable options and a local scheme in an LIC/NEE

keywords.def: supplying water to crops by pipes, channels or sprinklers
growing plants in nutrient-rich water without soil
using improved seeds, biotechnology and sustainable methods to raise yields

simple, affordable technology suited to local needs

starter: Bismillah. Name two impacts of food insecurity.
Define food security.
What is irrigation?

teach.heading: Strategies to increase supply

head: Strategy
How it works
Pros and cons
rows: More yield; can lower water tables and cause salt build-up
High yield and little land; high energy and set-up cost
High-yield seeds, fertiliser and better methods
Higher output; chemical use and cost
Crops modified for yield or resistance
Higher yields; ethical and ownership concerns
Hand pumps, drip kits, simple tools

teach.note: Use the table and ask pupils to rank them by cost, scale and sustainability. The new green revolution builds on the 1960s green revolution (high-yielding varieties, for example IR8 rice, with fertiliser and irrigation) but aims to reduce environmental damage. GM crops are debated: Golden Rice was approved in the Philippines in 2021 but its approval was later suspended by a court in 2024 (verify).

teach.heading: Large-scale development: Almeria, Spain
bullets: South-east Spain, an area with very low rainfall.
About 30,000 hectares of plastic greenhouses (approx.).
Grows tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers for export to northern Europe.

left.title: Advantages
points: Thousands of jobs and local income

right.title: Disadvantages
points: Low pay and poor conditions for some migrant workers

teach.note: Teacher to verify area and tonnage (reports vary). Use imagery of the 'sea of plastic'. Ask pupils: why is a dry area good for greenhouses? (Abundant sunshine, mild winters.) Water comes from groundwater and desalination, drip irrigation reduces waste.

teach.heading: Check and model

check.q: Why is Almeria suitable for large-scale greenhouse farming?
options: It has plenty of sunshine and mild winters
check.why: Almeria has high sunshine and mild winters, so growing continues all year. It is dry, which causes water problems.

teach.note: Answer B. Use the model to build a case-study paragraph.

teach.heading: Model: evaluate a development

model.problem: Evaluate a large-scale agricultural development you have studied. (6 marks)
steps: Positive: Almeria's greenhouses produce vegetables year-round for export, creating jobs.
Positive: drip irrigation and high yields use water and land efficiently.
Negative: groundwater has been over-abstracted, and desalination is needed.
Negative: plastic waste and low-paid migrant labour create environmental and social costs.
Judgement: the scheme is economically successful but not fully sustainable because water and social issues remain.
model.answer: A balanced judgement with place detail.

teach.note: Model use of place-specific detail.

teach.heading: Sustainable options and a local scheme
teach.note: Organic farming, permaculture, urban farming (for example Growing Underground in disused tunnels beneath Clapham, London) and food-waste reduction (UK households throw away around 6 million tonnes of food a year; approx., WRAP). Local scheme: floating gardens in Bangladesh, where flood-prone communities grow vegetables on rafts of water hyacinth and bamboo; NGOs such as Practical Action have supported them (teacher to verify districts and statistics). Benefits: food in the flood season, low cost, organic compost; limits: small scale.

practice: Describe two strategies for increasing food supply. (2 marks)
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of hydroponics. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how the new green revolution can increase food supply. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain one benefit and one cost of Almeria's greenhouses. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of a local scheme in an LIC or NEE in increasing sustainable food supply. (6 marks)
exit: Define hydroponics.
Name one sustainable food option.
lessons.homework: Design a poster explaining how a school could reduce food waste, with three actions and expected results.

energy sources that will run out, such as coal, oil and gas
energy sources that are naturally replenished, such as wind and solar

the total greenhouse gases produced by a person, product or activity

What is the energy mix?
Name two renewable sources.

bullets: China and the USA are the biggest total consumers.
Per person, HICs and oil-rich states use far more than LICs.
About 80% of world energy is still from fossil fuels (approx.).

head: Pattern
Detail (approx.)
rows: Oil, coal and gas still about 80%

Show a map of energy use per person: Canada, USA and Gulf states high; Sub-Saharan Africa low; about 750 million people lack electricity (IEA, approx. 2022). Distinguish total and per capita. cycle: Demand for electricity and fuel rises
Need for new sources or efficiency
teach.note: Make a causal chain with three drivers: population, industrialisation of NEEs and rising wealth (more cars, appliances, air conditioning). Ask: how can efficiency offset growth? Check.

teach.heading: Supply factors

head: Factor
Example
rows: Oil concentrated in the Middle East
Offshore wind and nuclear are expensive to build
Fracking opened new gas supply in the USA
2022 gas crisis after the war in Ukraine

teach.note: Link geography (location of reserves, e.g. oil in the Middle East, coal in China), cost (extraction and building new plants), technology (fracking, offshore wind) and politics (OPEC, wars). Example: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 reduced gas supplies to Europe and raised prices, leading to the UK Energy Price Guarantee (approx.). Ask pupils to classify each factor.

teach.heading: Impacts of energy insecurity

check.q: Which is an impact of energy insecurity on an economy?
options: Higher costs for businesses and households
check.why: Insecurity raises prices and costs, reducing output and household budgets. The other options describe secure supply.

teach.note: Sensitive areas: drilling in the Arctic or rainforest risks spills (the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill released about 4 million barrels of oil; approx.). Economies: rising bills push families into fuel poverty and reduce industrial output. Conflict: competition for oil and gas. Pupils should give specific examples. Use the check.

teach.heading: Comparing energy sources

head: Source
Type
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Flexible fuel; gas cleaner than coal
Dams flood land and displace people

teach.note: Ask pupils to use the table to judge each source on cost, reliability and environmental impact. Nuclear low-carbon but costly with waste storage issues. Wind and solar are intermittent. Hydro is reliable but dams alter ecosystems. Misconception: renewables have no impact: they affect wildlife and land.

practice: Describe the global pattern of energy consumption. (2 marks)
Explain two reasons why global energy demand is increasing. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how politics can affect energy supply. (3 marks)
Extend: Compare one renewable and one non-renewable energy source. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impacts of energy insecurity. (6 marks)
exit: Define energy security.
Give one advantage of nuclear power.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Energy option (AQA 3.2.3.4; option, one of food, water or energy)
lessons.title: OPTION: Energy. Fossil fuel extraction (Alberta), sustainable options and a local renewable scheme

objectives: Describe and evaluate the extraction of a fossil fuel: the Alberta oil sands
Explain sustainable options: conservation, design, demand reduction and cleaner fossil fuels
Describe a local renewable scheme in an LIC/NEE
successCriteria: All: describe the Alberta oil sands and one advantage and disadvantage
Most: explain sustainable energy options
Some: evaluate a local renewable scheme
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: fuels and carbon; Design Technology: efficient buildings
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of the Earth (khalifah) and avoiding waste (Qur'an 7:31)

keywords.def: sand or clay containing thick oil called bitumen, which must be separated before use
capturing carbon dioxide from power plants and storing it underground
using less energy through efficiency and behaviour
a small hydroelectric scheme generating power for a village
building and product design that uses less energy and resources

starter: Bismillah. Name two impacts of energy insecurity.
Define non-renewable.
Why is renewable energy not always fully sustainable?

teach.heading: Alberta oil sands
bullets: Northern Alberta, Canada, around Fort McMurray.
Canada has the world's third-largest proven oil reserves, mostly oil sands (approx.).
Production around 3 to 3.5 million barrels a day (approx.).

left.title: Advantages
points: Jobs in Fort McMurray and across Canada

right.title: Disadvantages
points: Boreal forest cleared and tailings ponds
Risks to Indigenous communities and wildlife

teach.note: Teacher to verify with the Alberta Energy Regulator and Natural Resources Canada. Methods: open-pit mining and in situ steam drilling (SAGD). Ask pupils to describe the scale of change in the boreal forest. Mention Indigenous communities such as Fort Chipewyan living downstream; concerns about water and health continue.

teach.heading: Model: weigh up an example

model.problem: Evaluate the extraction of a fossil fuel you have studied. (6 marks)
steps: Economic: the Alberta oil sands support thousands of jobs and large export income.
Social: Fort McMurray grew rapidly, but the 2016 wildfire forced about 88,000 people to leave (approx.).
Environmental: forest loss, tailings ponds and high carbon emissions per barrel.
Counter: technology such as carbon capture and land reclamation can reduce impacts.
Judgement: economic benefits are large but environmental costs are serious, so the case for extraction depends on stricter controls.
model.answer: A balanced judgement with detail and conclusion.

teach.note: Show how to give a balanced paragraph with place detail.

teach.heading: Sustainable energy options
teach.note: Use the table to link each option to action at home, school and government level. Examples: UK building regulations, LED bulbs, insulation, smart meters. Link to Islam: avoid israf (waste), Qur'an 7:31.

cycle: Falls through a pipe to a turbine
Village gets electricity for lights and mills
Schools, health posts and small businesses benefit
